Published online:
September 9, 2026

Geographic focus:
United States

Temporal focus:
T1. Historical report [NO]
T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES]
T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [YES]

Synopsis:
A Reuters poll of 93 economists shows ~70% expect the Fed to hold rates at 3.50%-3.75% at the Sept 15-16 FOMC meeting, down sharply from 90% in August. Hawkish signals from Fed Chair Warsh at Jackson Hole, oil above $100/barrel, 10Y yields near 5%, and sticky PCE inflation well above the 2% target have significantly shifted the distribution of risk toward hikes. Roughly 44% now expect at least one hike in 2026, more than double last month's share. PCE inflation is not expected to return to 2% before 2028.

Q01. Is the content's main message on the US economy, US yields, US interest rates?
Relevance: YES

Q02. Is the content about increasing US interest rates?
Relevance: 75 (heavily featured as the primary risk scenario, with momentum clearly building toward a hike)
Probability of increase: 30% (implied by ~30% of polled economists expecting a near-term hike, corroborated by market pricing of two hikes by March and hawkish Fed rhetoric)

Q03. Is the content about holding stable US interest rates?
Relevance: 70 (still the base case, but conviction is visibly eroding)
Probability of holding: 56% (directly stated — 52 of 93 economists expect no change for the full year; 65 of 93 for the next meeting specifically maps to ~70% for the immediate meeting)

Q04. Is the content about decreasing US interest rates?
Relevance: 5 (mentioned only as a fringe outlier — one single contributor, Jefferies, expects a cut)
Probability of decrease: 1%

Q05. Focus on the very latest information: What is the sentiment/tone including the very latest information on US interest rates?
Sentiment: +65 (distinctly more hawkish than before — Warsh's Jackson Hole speech perceived as hawkish, 10Y yields near the politically sensitive 5% threshold, oil back above $100, market pricing two hikes by March, and the share of economists forecasting at least one hike has more than doubled month-over-month; the base case remains a hold but the risk skew has shifted materially to the upside on rates)
